red.focus: Translate conditional rules into clear reasoning
red.summary: Many duties operate only when specified facts exist. Learn the logical difference between a necessary condition and a sufficient condition in legal language.
checklist: I can identify an if-then rule
I can distinguish necessary and sufficient conditions
I can avoid reversing a conditional statement

sections.title: Read the Direction of a Rule
sections.body_md: A law says, 'If a company stores personal data, it must follow specified security rules.' That tells us a condition triggering duties for covered companies. It does not tell us that only those companies have any security duties under all laws. The implication has a direction: when the condition is satisfied, a specified result follows under the law. A beginner should write both parts explicitly and avoid inventing the reverse proposition.
sections.audio_script: A law says, 'If a company stores personal data, it must follow specified security rules.' That tells us a condition triggering duties for covered companies. A beginner should write both parts explicitly and avoid inventing the reverse proposition.

sections.title: Necessary and Sufficient
sections.body_md: A sufficient condition is enough to trigger a consequence under a given rule; a necessary condition must be present for that consequence to follow under the stated framework. A valid permit may be necessary to operate a regulated service, but having a permit may not be sufficient if other duties remain. The difference can decide whether a legal argument is valid. A careful lawyer asks whether the proposed fact is required, enough by itself, or merely relevant.

sections.title: Exceptions Need Their Own Place
sections.body_md: An ordinance may state a general duty and then exempt emergency services. If the exception applies, the conclusion changes. The reasoning is not inconsistent; the premise was incomplete without the exemption. A legal analyst should list the duty's trigger, required behavior, exclusions and consequences. This structure makes complex provisions understandable without sacrificing accuracy. It also prevents an advocate from imposing a duty on someone the rule explicitly excludes.

yellow.focus: Recognize quantifier errors in legal rules
yellow.summary: Words such as all, some, only and unless can determine whether a conclusion follows. Learn how broad generalizations fail when a legal condition has been overlooked.
checklist: I can distinguish universal from existential claims
I can translate an only-if clause correctly

sections.title: All and Some Are Not Interchangeable
sections.body_md: A rule might protect all qualifying consumers who purchased defective products. It does not follow that every person who bought any product qualifies. The quantifier all applies within the defined class, not to the entire population. A legal analysis should identify the relevant set, its defining conditions and any exclusions. A tiny shift from 'all eligible applicants' to 'all applicants' can turn a true statute summary into false advice.

sections.title: Only If Points to Necessity
sections.body_md: If a statute says a benefit is available only if the applicant is resident, residency is a necessary condition. It does not by itself prove that every resident receives the benefit; further conditions may apply. This is a common logical mistake in arguments about eligibility and entitlement. Rewrite the sentence explicitly before applying it. Careful attention to only if and if reduces avoidable errors in rules involving multiple requirements.

sections.title: One Counterexample Matters
sections.body_md: A claim that 'courts always award damages after any breach' can be defeated by a valid example where a remedy is legally unavailable. Some arguments need only one counterexample to refute an overly broad universal statement. Other claims concern probabilities and require a different kind of evidence. The lawyer should identify the logical form before searching for proof. This avoids treating a single anecdote as conclusive about a statistical trend or ignoring a genuine exception to a universal rule.

orange.focus: Model complex duties with exceptions and rule conflicts
orange.summary: Advanced legal arguments often involve rules that apply generally but yield to narrower provisions. Analyze defeasible conditions and priority without treating legal interpretation as an automatic calculation.
checklist: I can identify general rule and specific exception
I can recognize apparent conflicts between duties
I can explain where the legal system supplies priority rules

sections.title: A General Duty May Be Defeated
sections.body_md: A professional must ordinarily preserve client confidentiality, but applicable law may authorize or require disclosure in specifically defined circumstances. The initial duty remains meaningful while its application changes when the exception's elements are proved. Defeasible reasoning makes this explicit: a conclusion holds unless a legally recognized defeater applies. A lawyer must identify the actual source and scope of any exception rather than infer one from moral intuition.

sections.title: Rules Can Appear to Conflict
sections.body_md: A public body may face a general disclosure duty alongside a specific statute protecting certain records. Depending on the jurisdiction, a valid rule may give the specific protection priority, or other conflict rules may apply. The argument must identify hierarchy, timing, specificity and any controlling precedent. These are legal source questions, not merely mathematical contradictions. The best analysis demonstrates why the legal order selects one duty or reconciles them.

sections.title: Burden of Proof Is Part of the Structure
sections.body_md: Some exceptions must be raised by a respondent; others form part of what a claimant must establish. Those procedural allocations vary. A formal logical model can show how an exception changes the conclusion but cannot decide who bears the burden without legal authority. An advanced lawyer maps the duty's conditions, the exception's elements, the evidence and the procedural rule. This yields a more accurate prediction than either a rigid slogan or an unstructured plea for fairness.

black.focus: Critique automation of duty reasoning under contested premises
black.summary: At doctoral depth, examine the promise and risk of formal rule engines for complex legal duties. Design systems that distinguish certain rules, contested interpretations and human decisions.
checklist: I can model defeasible rules without false certainty
I can evaluate hidden assumptions in automated compliance
I can propose accountable human review of conflicts

sections.title: Code Can Follow a Bad Rule Perfectly
sections.body_md: An automated benefits system may deny an application because it treats one supporting document as mandatory when the statute permits alternatives. The software's internal logic might be flawless, but its legal premise is wrong. A doctoral analyst must distinguish computational correctness from correct interpretation and authority. Every rule should be traceable to an authentic source and version, with exceptions represented explicitly. People affected need a meaningful route to challenge both data and legal meaning.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution Needs Legitimacy
sections.body_md: Two obligations may genuinely compete: confidentiality and disclosure, security and expression, administrative efficiency and individualized hearing. A programmed priority cannot simply be the designer's moral preference. The legal system may provide hierarchy, proportionality, explicit exceptions or discretionary judgment. A well-designed rule engine should flag unresolved conflicts for qualified review rather than silently select one. This reduces the risk that an opaque tool assumes powers no institution lawfully granted it.

sections.title: Human Review Must Be Real
sections.body_md: A nominal appeals button does little if reviewers cannot see the rule, evidence or machine reasoning that produced a decision. A robust design needs versioned legal sources, transparent reasons, review procedures and correction of recurring errors. It must protect personal data and avoid making vulnerable users prove that an inaccessible algorithm is wrong. The goal is not to reject automation but to place it within accountable legal institutions that respect dignity, accuracy and the right to be heard.
